title: Wealth and sacrifice cannot match God's righteousness
english: So let wealth and glory be reckoned as nothing great—at least, the things that do not depart together with the one who acquired them, as righteousness does depart with him and brings back those who have been brought low.

The heavenly perfect races, he says, will sing in praise of God's righteousness, applauding with perfect words that possess what is most just and most discerning: that God is gladdened not by sacrifices but by judgment, and holds this as his everlasting covenant (Ps 49:6; Ps 49:13).

For God is not in need of food and drink, he says, that he should attend to meats as food and to blood as drink. Then, introducing the true honor of God in place of the name of sacrifice, he adds what follows.
Consider this to be sacrifice, he says: the awareness of benefits, the confession from the heart, and the fulfillment of prayers as a debt owed by human beings to God (Ps 49:14).

And if you do these things, he says, be of good hope that you will obtain God as your helper in afflictions, so that you may also glorify him when you are benefited, offering thanks without ceasing (Ps 49:15; Ps 49:17).

These things are a paralysis of the law: the commandment “You shall not steal” is paralyzed by running together with a thief; “You shall not commit adultery” by being arrayed with adulterers; “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” and “You shall not go about in deceit among your nation” by speaking conspiratorial and deceitful words, by accusing, and by devising stumbling blocks for a neighbor (Ps 49:21).

But the judgment will reveal the knowledge, because I will make you yourself visible to yourself. For each person will see himself, when hearts are uncovered, as he was formed from his heart. And Theodotion, rendering “I will add, I will heap up,” indicated the sudden gathering of deeds that comes before the eyes of the one who did them (Ps 50:5).

This was the “righteous accuser of himself.” For I do not wait, he says, for the reproof of another, even though the prophet did reprove me. He did so once, but I see my offense continually—yet I do not despair of healing, because of mercy.

This is a request for pardon, because sin has grown together with us from our first origin, passed on to us from the mothers who conceive us (Ps 50:7). For “through one man sin entered the world” (Romans 5:12), and evil was rooted in the first woman, and from her it passes through childbirth to those who are born. This is said more fittingly of the mother, even though sin also comes through the father, because we are brought forth from the father in seed, but from mothers completely, and we come into the light through childbirth.

We, he says, have been rooted in lawlessness and are born in sins, but what pleases you is what is truly good and in no way distorted. How then can human beings be glorified before such a judge, rather than carry away shame by being condemned? (Ps 50:8a)

From the grace that already existed toward him, he asks that sparing may also now come about. For God brings what follows upon the beginnings that come from himself, for the sake of his own purpose and steadfastness, even if what comes from us is not entirely worthy—just as, for the sake of the covenant with Abraham, he has mercy on the race descended from him when it suffers harm, bringing what follows upon the beginning and guarding the certainty of the promise above the equality of authority. Since, then, he knows he has obtained wisdom from God and has been honored by it, so as to understand even the hidden things about which he prays—“Open my eyes, and I will consider the wonders of your law” (Psalm 118:18 [119:18])—for this reason he acknowledges gratitude for the gift of wisdom, and asks that God remove the defilement that has come upon him, adding this also to grace.

The Savior said that Abraham, expecting his day, rejoiced beforehand, and when it came he saw it and rejoiced—Abraham, as he says, “your father rejoiced that he might see my day, and he saw it and was glad” (John 8:56). But David speaks of hearing instead of sight, saying that he will hear in Hades the cause of great gladness—the coming of the Savior signified to him by the Spirit—and that he will rejoice in Hades in spirit, and his bones within the tombs, humbled by sin and death, will also rejoice together with him, since the body that is the cause of resurrection was buried with them (Ps 50:10).

Sin is weak and a cause of weakness, but righteousness is strong, and so is God, its champion. Such also is hope in God, and especially the unceasing hope. And just as hope is understood from the first origin as something that could not have existed without God, so when it stands against the opposition of painful things, it is trained all the more (Ps 70:7).

orientation: Apollinaris is commenting on Psalm 49 (50), explaining that God desires thanksgiving and trust rather than sacrifices, and that sin is inherited from the first generation.

title: God's strength in old age and Christ's righteous kingdom
english: Since in the season of youth I took your help, not bodily vigor, as my strength, let this strength remain with me even as youth fades, and when human strength has passed away entirely, let the power that comes from you stand by me—as it did for David himself in old age (Ps 70:9). For when he was young, his son rose up against him, but when he was old, no one did. Chilled already by old age and lying helpless on his bed, he still ruled Israel and gave orders to the nation. He ruled Israel and appointed Solomon as his successor, after casting out Adonijah, who had tried to reign against his will.

These words would fit the time of Absalom's rebellion, the time about which those other words were spoken in Psalm 3: “Many say of my soul, ‘There is no salvation for him in his God’” (Psalm 3:2). And by his fellowship with the righteous, the Lord also suffered this kind of rebellion from his enemies, who said, “Let him be delivered, since he delights in him” (Psalm 22:8), and who thought that the one suffering according to the Father's will had been abandoned. So let the wicked, he says, fail in their purpose, and let the matter turn out according to my hope, not according to their supposition.
Do not be far from me, but hasten your help and turn their boasting into shame, so that my hope may increase all the more, and my hymns to you as well (Ps 70:12).

Symmachus says, “I do not know how to count them out.” For since he had promised to recount God's righteousness and the salvation that had come to him, and the promise was greater than what belongs to a human being, he added these words.

He begins the hymn at the very point where he had promised, doing it immediately, crying out with a loud voice the height of God's wonders: that human beings who had been brought through many afflictions attain good things in eternal life, having risen from the dead. This is the chief point of the divine hymns and the clearest demonstration of God, since none of those who are called gods could rival it. For God is the one who gives life to all things, and in him Christ is known, being the Son of God, saying that he himself is the resurrection and the life (John 11:25) and showing this in deed. So even if these words are spoken by Christ as a human being to the Father, it is fitting that they be spoken to him as well by human beings, as to the Son and image of God. For he is the firstborn from the dead, having descended in the manner of a human being, but having ascended by the power of God, being himself the author of the ascent, as he says to the Jews, in which the excellence of his divinity is shown.
Even if you made your great power manifest by handing human nature over to death, yet to the one despaired of among human beings you gave back a new and blessed life.

The glory of Christ after the passion is hymned. Solomon is a type: the peace of his kingdom, the protection of the righteous, the glory of his wisdom, and the honor he received from all people. But beyond the type is this: that the days of the king endure to the consummation, and his peace and his fruit become most brilliant. For these things in no way fit Solomon, who lived only a short time, had opponents, and left no fruit from himself except one son—and that son did not preserve the kingdom handed down to him. But Christ's power is perpetual and unshaken, and his fruit is most glorious: those who believe. And the other things that came to pass in a typical way in Solomon are more perfectly fulfilled in him, as the discourse will explain point by point. “O God, give your judgment to the king, and your righteousness to the king's son, to judge your people in righteousness and your poor in judgment” (Ps 71:1,2). The Lord Christ is both king and son of King David according to the flesh, and for this reason he arose from the royal line, so that he might set right the ancestral kingdom according to Isaiah's prophecy, make it divine instead of human, and—what did not exist in any human kingdom—apply the exactness of righteousness to his subjects and grant to the wronged that they not be wronged. For not even in David himself was this preserved. Even though he was most righteous and pleasing to God beyond others, he still became the perpetrator of injustice against Uriah. And Solomon's case was even greater injustice, stretching into impiety through the making of idols. But this is the king foretold through Isaiah and Jeremiah: a righteous king seated on a throne established with mercy, judging and seeking judgment and hastening righteousness, as Isaiah says (Isaiah 16:5), and understanding and doing judgment and righteousness, as Jeremiah says (Jeremiah 23:5).

title: Symmachus and the prophets on the nations' tribute and the end of David's prayers
english: Symmachus rendered it, “And they will fear him as long as the sun endures” (Ps 72:5), in agreement with what Gabriel said to the holy virgin: “The Lord will give him the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever” (Psalm 71 [72]) (Ps 71:10-11).

Isaiah also says these things to Jerusalem: “The wealth of the sea and of nations and peoples will turn to you; herds of camels will come, and the camels of Midian will cover you; elephants will come from Sheba bearing gold, and they will bring frankincense, and they will proclaim the salvation of God.” And through Haggai it is said: “Once more I will shake heaven and earth and sea and dry land, and I will shake all the nations; and the chosen things of all the nations will come, and I will fill this house with glory, says the Lord Almighty” (Haggai 2:6-7) (Ps 71:16).
For the whole inhabited world is luxuriant and has blossomed with the fruit of Christ, and an uncountable multitude of Christ’s children appears in every city like grass from the earth (Ps 71:20).

Here, then, David’s prayers are fulfilled—the prayers he made for the eternal permanence of the throne when he said: “Lord, the word you spoke concerning the house of your servant and concerning your servant, let it be made faithful forever; and do as you have spoken, and let your name be exalted forever, while they say, ‘The Lord Almighty is the God of Israel,’ and the house of David your servant is raised up.” Unreasonably, then, was the heading written on the next psalm: “The hymns of David son of Jesse are ended.” For this psalm is the end of that collection, and part of the thanksgiving for the fulfillment of David’s prayers.

The second book of psalms also ended with a blessing that sounds out the “Amen,” just as the first book’s “May it be” makes clear, as has been said. For the end of that first book was Psalm 40, spoken in reference to Christ, and the end of this second book is the one just mentioned, Psalm 71. The third book ends—so that I may speak about it now as well—at Psalm 88, so that there are in all 17 psalms, of which 11 are by Asaph, then 4 by the sons of Korah, 1 by David, and Heman the Israelite’s is last.

Instead of “They passed through into the disposition of the heart,” Aquila rendered, “They passed by the watchtowers of the heart.” This means they are unwilling to carry out any of their natural thoughts, nor do they practice what they understand to be good, but they turn away from these things. Virtue is a joke to them; slander against their inferiors comes easily; blasphemy against God is ready at hand; their tongue is quick against human beings. And this is what “their tongue passed through upon the earth” means (Ps 72:11, 13).

The righteous [will be blessed] in the future state, as Jeremiah also says something of this kind: “If you turn back, I will restore you before my face” (Jeremiah 15:19). There he says, “And all who planned evil, who chose evil, will change their minds.” For when the good things appear among the race of the righteous, they will say, “There is, then, a providence of God; and how does he know what is done?” This is the voice of those who have lost their natural reasoning because of the good things that came to them unprofitably, leading them into injustices. For prospering contrary to reason produces thoughts that the world is not governed according to reason, nor will he know our [the text is damaged here; perhaps: hardships]. But although providence stands over all things, nevertheless, he says, these impious people, who are unbearable in their arrogance and in their words against God even amid their good cheer, and who are not yet persuaded by the approval of the righteous—they mock [the text is damaged here] the one who is steadfast of hands [perhaps: clean of hands, as in Psalm 72:13] as a vain steadfastness, and they speak evil of the one who chooses righteousness. This is the difficulty of human reasoning: to repent of zeal for virtue as though it were not good or profitable. Such thoughts often enter many people’s minds, and he intends to heal them by his word. To destroy the impious reasoning, he confirms the more pious reasoning through the person of God. For what is said truly requires God as guarantor: that the pious who now suffer hardship are more blessed in the future state than the impious who prosper to the end. Such is the saying in Jeremiah: “If you turn back, I will restore you before my face” (Jeremiah 15:19). And “They said, ‘How does God know?’” is the voice of those who have lost their natural reasoning through unprofitable luxury; for if providence exists, they would not prosper while the good suffer hardship (Ps 72:24).

Symmachus later said, “Honor received me.” And in another sense: I rested, knowing to be silent and to trust you as the one who governs our affairs well, and so to be with you always; therefore you took hold of me; you placed good glory in me, you brought me to blessed glory (Ps 73:4).
The mention of the places is necessary because of the people’s lawlessness.
